record.paper_title: $p$-matchings in graphs: a brief survey with some open problems
record.original_question: Let G=(V,E) be a finite graph and let M⊆E be a matching. Write G[M] for the subgraph induced by all endpoints of edges in M. For a graph property P, call M a P-matching when G[M] has property P, and call a P-matching maximum when its cardinality is as large as possible among all P-matchings of G. For each P-matching variant defined by such a property P, develop characterization theorems that determine exactly when a given P-matching M is maximum.

evidence.quote: Definition 3.1. Let P be a property of G, and let M a matching of G such that the induced subgraph of M, <M>, has property P, then we call M a P-matching.
Also for each P-matching, characterization theorems should be developed to describe when a given matching M is a maximum P-matching.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph. A matching of $G$ is a set $M\subseteq E$ of pairwise non-adjacent edges. Write $\langle M\rangle$ for the subgraph of $G$ induced by the set of all endpoints of edges in $M$. Given a graph property $P$ (i.e., a class of graphs closed under isomorphism), a matching $M$ of $G$ is called a $P$-matching if $\langle M\rangle$ has property $P$. A $P$-matching $M$ is called a maximum $P$-matching of $G$ if $|M|\ge|M'|$ for every $P$-matching $M'$ of $G$.

For each graph property $P$ of interest (for instance: "is an induced matching" (i.e., $\langle M\rangle$ consists of independent edges), "has $M$ as its unique perfect matching" (uniquely restricted matching), "is connected", "is disconnected", "is acyclic", and other natural choices), develop a structural characterization theorem giving necessary and sufficient conditions, in terms of $G$ and $M$, for a given $P$-matching $M$ of $G$ to be a maximum $P$-matching of $G$. Analogous to the Berge-type characterization of maximum matchings via the nonexistence of augmenting paths, the goal is to identify, for each property $P$, the combinatorial obstruction whose absence is equivalent to maximality of $M$ as a $P$-matching.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is a broad program: provide Berge-type characterizations of maximum $P$-matchings for each graph property $P$. While certain specific variants have partial characterizations (e.g., graphs in which every maximum matching is uniquely restricted have been characterized, and conditions for equality of induced matching number and matching number are known), a uniform body of characterization theorems for arbitrary $P$ does not appear in the literature. For most $P$-matching variants such as induced, uniquely restricted, and acyclic matchings, deciding maximality is NP-hard in general, and no Berge-type structural characterization is known. The general program therefore remains open.

status_evidence.title: Uniquely Restricted Matchings
status_evidence.snippet: Graphs in which every maximum matching is uniquely restricted have been characterized.
status_evidence.claim: Partial characterization results exist for specific P-matching variants, but only for restricted graph classes/properties.

status_evidence.title: On some hard and some tractable cases of the maximum acyclic matching problem
status_evidence.snippet: The maximum acyclic matching problem is NP-hard in general with tractable cases in restricted classes.
status_evidence.claim: For several P-matching variants the decision problem is NP-hard, suggesting no simple uniform Berge-type characterization is known.

status_evidence.title: Maximum Induced Matching Algorithms via Vertex Ordering Characterizations
status_evidence.snippet: Vertex ordering characterizations are used for maximum induced matchings only in specific graph classes.
status_evidence.claim: Characterizations of maximum induced matchings are known only for special graph classes, not in general.
